Specifically, the court stated:

"However, in his submissions he raised an objection. Which in his opinion, if the taxing master would have considered, would probably have reached a different decision. In light of Article 159 (2) (d) that states that “justice will be done without undue regard to procedural technicalities” I will consider the response in the submissions as objections raised. With paragraph 22 above in mind, does invoking natural justice and Fair hearing under Article 50 and 47 of the constitution ousters the provision of paragraph 11? I think not. Although the Applicant has framed the application as one alleging an error apparent on the face of the record and denial of a fair hearing, the effect of the application seeks to impeach and set aside the decision of the taxing officer. Such a challenge fall within the ambit of Paragraph 11 of the Advocates (Remuneration) Order. And thus, the issues of natural justice and fair hearing as raised can be well articulated in the bounds of paragraph 11 of the advocates Renumeration order." [chunk_id: Kariithi v GN Thiongo Associates (Miscellaneous Application E262of2025) 2026KEHC11082(KLR) (22July2026) (Ruling)__s2__c21]

expected_value: A court will normally not interfere with a Taxing Officer's decision unless it is based on an error of principle, which can be inferred if the sum awarded is manifestly excessive, or if there was a misdirection resulting in a wrong decision. The basis for determining subject matter value for instruction fees is wholly dependent on the stage at which the fees are being taxed.
answer:
According to the legal principles cited, a court will not normally interfere with the exercise of discretion by the taxing officer unless the taxing officer erred in principle in assessing the costs [chunk_id: Johnson Kibunja Njoka  another v Joseph Njuguna  2 others 2017KEHC6481(KLR)__s2__c14]. Questions solely of quantum are regarded as matters with which the taxing officers are particularly fitted to deal, and the court will interfere only in exceptional cases [chunk_id: Johnson Kibunja Njoka  another v Joseph Njuguna  2 others 2017KEHC6481(KLR)__s2__c14].

For the determination of the subject matter value for instruction fees, it is wholly dependent on the stage at which the fees are being taxed. Before judgment, the pleadings form the basis for determining the subject value. Once judgment has been entered, the judgment determines conclusively the value of the subject matter as a claim, regardless of how it was pleaded [chunk_id: Njeri v Mathenge (Civil Appeal 5of2017) 2022KEHC14977(KLR) (2November2022) (Ruling)__s2__c3, chunk_id: Gikaria ta Anthony Gikaria  Company Advocates v Samchi Telecommunications Limited (Environment and Land Miscellaneous Case E008of2025) 2025KEELC18295(KLR) (13November2025) (Ruling)__s2__c23, chunk_id: Kamau  another v Ali  another (Environment and Land Miscellaneous Case 150of2024) 2026KEELC1365(KLR) (26February2026) (Ruling)__s2__c2].

faithfulness_reasoning: The answer accurately states that a court interferes only where the taxing officer erred in principle, with quantum issues disturbed only exceptionally, and correctly explains that subject matter value for instruction fees depends on the stage of taxation: pleadings before judgment and the judgment itself after judgment.

answer:
In GKM v MNK (Originating Summons 1of2018) 2024KEHC54(KLR) (10January2024) (Ruling), the judge defined "sufficient reason" under Order 45 Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Rules as a reason which in consideration of the interest of justice would justify the review, varying or setting aside of the order. The judge further elaborated that the phrase "sufficient reason" does not necessarily have to be analogous or ejusdem generis to the other reasons stipulated in Order 45 Rule 1. Instead, it can include any valid justification warranting a review to prevent injustice, such as procedural delays that undermine the fair administration of justice [chunk_id: GKM v MNK (Originating Summons 1of2018) 2024KEHC54(KLR) (10January2024) (Ruling)__s3__c5].

A court may interfere with a taxing officer's decision on the assessment of costs if the decision is based on an error of principle or if the fee awarded is manifestly excessive as to justify interference [chunk_id: LENNAH WANJIKU KOINANGE  V MAJANJA LUSENO  COMPANY ADVOCATES 2013KEHC4350(KLR)__s3__c5]. 

If the court finds that an error of principle has been committed, the normal practice is to remit the question of quantum for the decision of the taxing officer, unless the judge is satisfied that the error cannot materially have affected the assessment and the court is not entitled to upset the taxation because in its opinion, the amount awarded was high [chunk_id: Robert Muthawa v Eliud Munyika James 2017KEHC5862(KLR)__s0__c1].

In such cases, the court has discretion to deal with the matter if the justice of the case so requires, and the appropriate remedy is to remit the matter for fresh taxation before a different taxing officer [chunk_id: Mwangi ta Raydon Mwangi  Associates Advocates v Njenga (Miscellaneous Application E025of2024) 2026KEHC13078(KLR) (13August2026) (Ruling)__s3__c12].

faithfulness_reasoning: The answer accurately reflects the context by stating that interference is permitted only for an error of principle or a manifestly excessive award, and that the usual remedy is to remit the quantum for reassessment, often before a different taxing officer.

expected_value: The court must consider that an extension of time is an equitable remedy rather than a right, that the applicant bears the burden of laying a satisfactory basis for the delay, and that it must assess whether the respondents will suffer prejudice if the extension is granted.
answer:
According to the Supreme Court's guidelines in Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR, the court must consider the following factors when exercising its discretion to grant an extension of time:

1. Extension of time is not a right of a party. It is an equitable remedy that is only available to a deserving party at the discretion of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

2. A party who seeks for extension of time has the burden of laying a basis to the satisfaction of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

3. Whether the court should exercise the discretion to extend time, is a consideration to be made on a case to case basis [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

4. Whether there is a reasonable reason for the delay. The delay should be explained to the satisfaction of the court [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

5. Whether there will be any prejudice suffered by the respondents if the extension is granted [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

6. Whether the application has been brought without undue delay [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].

7. Whether in certain cases, like election petitions, public interest should be a consideration for extending time [chunk_id: Jiangxi Transportation Engineering Group Ltd v Karweru Co Advocates (Miscellaneous Application E011of2022) 2024KEELRC1873(KLR) (19July2024) (Ruling)__s2__c3, Nicholas Kiptoo Arap Korir Salat v Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission & 7 others (2014) eKLR].
correctness_reasoning: It correctly states that extension of time is an equitable remedy, that the applicant bears the burden of justifying the delay, and that the court must consider potential prejudice to the respondents.
faithfulness_reasoning: The answer is fully supported by the provided context and accurately reproduces the Supreme Court’s listed factors for extension of time, including that it is an equitable remedy, the applicant bears the burden of justification, and prejudice to the respondent must be considered.
